final_text:
Short answer: confounding and measurement.

Why all three look “harmful” in NHANES
- Energy (calorie) confounding and body size: Day-1 24‑h recall nutrients (sodium, potassium, magnesium) scale strongly with total energy intake. People who eat more calories tend to be heavier and have higher DBP. If you don’t energy-adjust nutrients and control for BMI/size, virtually every macronutrient/micronutrient will show a positive association with DBP.
- Collinearity of nutrients: Sodium, potassium, and magnesium intakes move together with total intake and with each other. Modeling them one-at-a-time (and without energy) makes each look positively related to DBP.
- Reverse causality and treatment: People with hypertension change diet, take supplements (K/Mg), and use BP meds. Cross-sectionally, they still have higher DBP on average, which can make K/Mg intakes appear positively associated.
- Measurement error: Single 24‑h recall (large within-person error, misreporting) and one-visit BP (noisy) bias associations and interact badly with energy confounding. Using absolute mg/day instead of usual intake magnifies this.
- Model choice: Many quick NHANES screens (including common EP-WAS settings) adjust for age/sex/ethnicity but not energy, BMI, meds, or diagnosis, so the calorie/BMI signal dominates.

How to make NHANES align with trials
- Use energy-adjusted intakes (mg per 1000 kcal or residual method) and include total energy as a covariate.
- Adjust for BMI (and often height/waist) and exclude or adjust for diagnosed hypertension and BP medications.
- Prefer biomarkers when possible: 24‑h urinary sodium and potassium, or at least the Na:K ratio; examine Na:K rather than sodium alone.
- Reduce measurement error: use both recall days and the NCI usual-intake method; remove implausible reporters.
- Model substitution/isocaloric analyses (e.g., higher K at fixed energy) or diet patterns (e.g., DASH score) rather than single absolute nutrients.
- Check secular-trend/Simpson’s paradox and run sensitivity analyses (exclude diagnosed; adjust for BMI/energy).

Bottom line: The “positive” DR1T nutrient → DBP findings in NHANES are artifacts of total energy/body size confounding, collinearity, reverse causality, and recall noise. When you energy-adjust, control for BMI/meds/diagnosis, and/or use urinary Na/K, the results converge with RCT evidence (higher sodium raises BP; higher potassium/magnesium lower or do not raise BP).

If you’d like, I can rerun these associations with energy-adjustment, BMI control, and hypertension exclusions, or use urinary Na:K where available, to show the correction.
